content: 1. 2. Key information regarding treatment, isolation, diagnostic facilities, and transportation for affected travelers must be documented. A list of all facilities designated to receive affected travelers from points of entry, including their names, addresses, contact details, distances, and route maps, should be created, regularly updated, and accessible to relevant personnel. 3. Progress, gaps, and plans for capacity development, including resources and timelines, should be documented by the competent authority or person responsible for the point of entry self-assessment. 4. Staff trained in infection control must be available on-site or on-call to examine affected animals. Infection control plans, including adequate equipment and procedures, should be prepared to manage heightened public health risks. 5. Arrangements for the referral and safe transport of animals to designated veterinary facilities must be documented. Administrative arrangements should include cleaning/disinfection equipment, supplies, and PPE for transport staff. 6. Designated spaces should be provided to interview suspected or affected travelers. These spaces must be hygienic, environmentally safe, and appropriately sized based on the volume and type of travelers. Independent exit passages should be available to transport suspected travelers to medical care facilities to prevent the spread of infection. Translation and interpreter services should be arranged when needed. 7. Personnel must be trained in the use of PPE for initial interviews and triage. 8. Facilities for the quarantine and assessment of suspected travelers should be located away from points of entry. An adequate number of trained personnel must be available to conduct interviews and provide timely first assessments of suspected travelers. Reporting procedures should be in place to notify competent authorities of events related to travelers that indicate infectious diseases or public health risks. 9. Administrative arrangements and formal agreements, such as memorandums of understanding, should be established with local or nearby hospitals, clinics, and health services to receive suspected travelers for quarantine and support services. These facilities should be equipped with necessary resources, including laboratory access, PPE, and trained personnel. 10. These locations must be designed to prevent harm to individuals and the environment, considering factors such as wind direction and proximity to human habitats. 11. PPE and training in its application should be provided to staff. 12.g., thermal scanners) should be implemented. Operational standards, training, and drills should be conducted to orient staff, including public health, airline, travel, security, and customs personnel, on their responsibilities for entry/exit controls. Reliable equipment must be calibrated and maintained, and personnel should be trained in its use and the interpretation of results. 13. A system should be in place to integrate exit screening results at airports with national surveillance and reporting systems for outbreaks of specified illnesses. Logistics, including baggage, security, and customs formalities, must be arranged for travelers, including suspected cases and asymptomatic contacts. 14. Arrangements for the safe and hygienic transport of suspected travelers to medical or quarantine facilities must be established. Transport services should have cleaning/disinfection equipment, supplies, and PPE for staff. Trained personnel must be available to transport suspected travelers according to technical requirements. 15. An Excel Spreadsheet File Model has been developed to facilitate the assessment of core capacity requirements at designated airports, ports, and ground crossings. This tool summarizes assessment results, calculates percentages, and provides initial data for developing work plans and monitoring implementation. The spreadsheet operates without macros, ensuring compatibility across operating systems. 16. The assessment process should be conducted by public health specialists knowledgeable about core capacity requirements under the International Health Regulations (IHR). The process involves document reviews, field observations, and the completion of the Core Capacity Assessment Tool. Results should be documented with comments, suggestions, and evidence such as photographs or videos. 17. The assessment tool includes modules for summarizing evaluation results, coordination and communication, routine core capacities, and response to public health emergencies of international concern (PHEIC). Results are calculated based on responses (Yes, No, or Partial) and expressed as percentages. These results are visually represented with color codes (red, yellow, green) to indicate areas needing improvement. 18. Worksheets in the Excel model can be protected to prevent unauthorized modifications. Assessors should save their work under a different name to preserve the original file. Final results, including strengths, weaknesses, and improvement plans, should be documented in the summary worksheet. 19. The evaluation of results should include input from assessors on areas requiring regulatory clarification or improvements to achieve full implementation of IHR core capacities.
